ONNX Runtime in-process#

-DONEBIT_ORT=ON links the distribution's ONNX Runtime into 1bit and builds two things on top of it: the 1bit ort-info probe, which reports the pin and the execution providers this binary really has, and libonebit_ep.so, a plugin execution provider that ORT loads by path at run time and that runs the graph's matmuls through the engine's own kernels.

It is off by default, and CI builds without it: it needs the libonnxruntime dev package, and nothing else in the engine depends on ONNX Runtime. ONNX Runtime is not modified, and the only constants this repository uses are the ones its public headers declare.

The pin#

what value
package Ubuntu 26.04 libonnxruntime1.23 + libonnxruntime-dev, 1.23.2+dfsg-6ubuntu1
library /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libonnxruntime.so.1.23.2
sha256 9c8f6112e9dcf09ed4e621a1d0a7b6ba49575c7d09f27a652d24a22c8564b13c
OrtApi v23, negotiated with OrtGetApiBase()->GetApi(ORT_API_VERSION)
pkg-config libonnxruntime (-I/usr/include/onnxruntime -lonnxruntime)
licence MIT, recorded in NOTICE (linked at build time, never redistributed)

The pin is a contract, not a preference: the plugin EP hands ORT a vtable of C function pointers whose layout is fixed by ORT_API_VERSION, so a host built for another version would call through the wrong offsets instead of failing. 1bit ort-info prints both numbers, and the version the headers compile against is checked against the version the loaded library serves.

Building it#

sudo apt install libonnxruntime-dev        # 1.23.2 on 26.04
cmake -S . -B build -DONEBIT_ORT=ON
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"
./build/1bit ort-info

That adds onnx/ to the build: the probe, libonebit_ep.so, and the two tests below. The build compiles against ORT 1.23's headers, so -DONEBIT_ORT=OFF produces a binary with no ORT symbols at all — the option is a compile-time switch, not a runtime one.

1bit ort-info#

onebit ort-info
  ortv    : 1.23.2
  api     : v23 (compile-time ORT_API_VERSION, negotiated above)
  lib     : /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libonnxruntime.so.1.23
  builtin : 3
            [0] DnnlExecutionProvider
            [1] XnnpackExecutionProvider
            [2] CPUExecutionProvider
  eproster: 1 (partition order; first EP gets the node, no tie-break)
            [0] CPUExecutionProvider  vendor=Microsoft  device=CPU

The two lists answer different questions. builtin is what is compiled into the .so the loader found — a distribution build carries DNNL and XNNPACK as well as the CPU EP, so "the CPU EP is the only provider" is not an assumption this build may make. eproster is the OrtEpDevice roster, and its order is the partition order: ORT offers a node to each provider in turn and the first one that returns a kernel gets it, with no tie-break. That is why every integration in this repository registers its own provider first and the CPU EP last.

The plugin EP#

libonebit_ep.so is a shared object ORT loads by path:

api->RegisterExecutionProviderLibrary(env, "onebit_ep", "/path/to/libonebit_ep.so");

Registration must happen before the session is created; GetEpDevices then returns one OrtEpDevice per hardware device the factory offers, and the caller appends them in the order it wants nodes partitioned. Unregistering invalidates those handles.

What it claims today, and the four edges ORT enforces on any plugin:

  • Ops. ONEBIT_EP_OPS (default MatMul). The rest of the target list — Gemm, Add, Softmax, LayerNormalization, RMSNorm, Gather — lands one at a time; anything unclaimed is offered to the next provider, so a graph never becomes unrunnable because of this EP.
  • Precision and rank. float32 only, rank 2 or 3 (ORT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED otherwise). No sync streams yet: an execution stream request fails cleanly rather than pretending.
  • Data transfer must be non-null. ORT calls through the vtable unconditionally, so a null CreateDataTransfer is a call to address 0. The allocator must be OrtDeviceAllocator and 256-byte aligned — MLAS loads assume it, and an arena allocator is refused by name.
  • Teardown. ReleaseEpFactory returns an OrtStatus* even though it "cannot fail"; ORT dereferences the result when it unloads the library, so returning void crashes at ReleaseEnv, long after the run that looked fine.

MatMul on the NPU#

With -DONEBIT_EP_NPU=ON and -DONEBIT_NPU_RT_DIR=<dir with npu_rt.cpp and npu_rt_api.cpp>, the same MatMul kernel calls the NPU through the forward route's I8Ctx — the same weight packer and the same activation quantiser the NPU lane uses (packB, per-row amax/127, readback and dequant by ascales[m] * group_scales[l][n]), so a device result is comparable with the forward route's. docs/npu.md covers the runtime and what ships in a release; the kernels are built one ELF per projection shape, and the ELF names its own geometry, which is why the shape is configuration rather than something the EP infers:

variable meaning
ONEBIT_EP_NPU_ELF the full-ELF kernel for this K and N (e.g. full_i8_O_K1024_N1024_m16.elf)
ONEBIT_EP_NPU_M, _K, _N the design dims that ELF was built for; a MatMul of another shape falls back to the host
ONEBIT_EP_TRACE=1 append one line per callback to /tmp/onebit_ep_trace.<pid>.log — the ownership evidence the tests read

The device lock. The NPU is shared, and the rule is that a plugin never evicts the owner's serve. The EP takes /tmp/1bit-npu-device.lock with flock(2) non-blocking and holds it for the life of the process; when the lock is held it does not queue — it reports device busy and runs the matmul on the host instead, because an inference session must not block on another process. The open itself matches app/npu_device_lock.h (engine#640): the fixed path, O_CREAT|O_RDONLY|O_NOFOLLOW at 0644, since a read fd is enough for flock and the path is not something an environment variable may name. The difference is only the contention policy — that helper queues by default, this one always gives up.

Numerics#

The two backends are held to different tolerances, because they compute different things: the host path is float32 and must match the CPU EP to 1e-5 relative; the device path is int8 by int8 into int32, and is held to 2e-2 of the result's magnitude. The proof prints which backend it got, so a silent fall back cannot be mistaken for a device pass.

Qwen3-0.6B#

The first real model through this path is Qwen3-0.6B, exported by onnx/export_qwen3.py into a plain graph — opset 20, ai.onnx domain only, float32, input_ids/attention_mask int64 [1, seq] in and logits float32 [1, seq, vocab] out, weights in one external-data sidecar. Attention is exported with attn_implementation="eager" on purpose: a fused/SDPA attention block hides the matmuls inside an op our EP does not claim, and then there is nothing to schedule.

python3 onnx/export_qwen3.py --model-dir ~/models/Qwen3-0.6B-hf --out ~/models/qwen3-0.6b.onnx --check
1bit ort-run --model ~/models/qwen3-0.6b.onnx --ep ./libonebit_ep.so --ids "9707 11 1879" -n 8 \
             --dump-logits /tmp/ort-logits
python3 onnx/compare_logits.py --forward /tmp/fwd-logits --ort /tmp/ort-logits

--check prints the operator census and every distinct MatMul (K, N) in the graph, which is both the EP's binding table and the coverage picture: 254 MatMul nodes in six shapes, of which this engine's kernels cover 1024 x 2048 (q) and 1024 x 1024 (k, v) — 84 nodes — and the rest stay on the CPU EP. ort-run therefore reports what it actually did: an EP-on-NPU run and an ONEBIT_EP_OPS=none control on the same graph, both with the CPU EP last.

The graph keeps no KV cache, so one decoding step re-runs the whole sequence: the tokens/s it prints is that graph's rate, and it is not comparable to a KV-cached server. The comparison that matters is against the forward route on the same token ids, which is what compare_logits.py does — per-step KL(forward || ort) in nats plus top-1 agreement, over the two logits dumps (decode_logits_idx<N>.bin from 1bit npu-run --dump-logits, logits_<N>.bin from ort-run). The measurements themselves are recorded in the state file for the deliverable, and the pack design they feed is in ONNX pack.

Two engines in one session#

The NPU EP is not the only accelerator worth registering. 1bit ort-run takes --ep once per library and applies them in the order given, with the CPU EP always last:

# our NPU EP first, a GPU EP (HIP/ROCM plugin, when one is installed) second, CPU last
1bit ort-run --model qwen3-0.6b.onnx \
    --ep ./libonebit_ep.so --ep /path/to/libhip_ep.so --ids "9707 11 1879 374" -n 16

Order is priority, and the two engines cover different halves of the same graph: the NPU takes the projection shapes it has an ELF for, the GPU EP takes what it supports, the CPU EP mops up. Two rules make this work, and one of them is a bug we hit:

  • each library is appended with its own SessionOptionsAppendExecutionProvider_V2 call — the API rejects a single call whose device list mixes two EPs (All OrtEpDevice values in ep_devices must have the same execution provider);
  • an EP must claim only what it can actually run. Our EP claims a MatMul only when both operands are float32 with rank 2 or 3, and with ONEBIT_EP_NPU only for (K, N) shapes an ELF is configured for and only while the device lock is ours. Claiming wider turned a graph that ran at 13 tokens/s on the CPU EP into one that ran at 0.18 tokens/s on our naive host kernel, and, before the rank check, into a graph that refused to run at all (only rank-2 and rank-3 MatMul are supported yet on a rank-4 attention matmul).

Quantised graphs (Quark A8W8 QDQ)#

A Quark-quantised ONNX model is a QDQ graph (DequantizeLinear → MatMul → QuantizeLinear with int8 tensors and float32 scales), and the MatMul inside it is the same int8 × int8 → int32 product our device kernel already computes. Such a graph runs on the EP unchanged today — the EP takes that MatMul and the surrounding DequantizeLinear/QuantizeLinear stay on the CPU EP — and the folding that removes the intermediate float tensors is designed in ONNX pack. ctest -R onebit_ep_qdq_proof checks the pattern end to end and requires int8-identical output.

Verifying#

cmake -S . -B build -DONEBIT_ORT=ON && cmake --build build -j && ctest --test-dir build -R "ort_info|onebit_ep"

Three tests, each proving a different claim:

test proves
ort_info the binary negotiated OrtApi v23 and can list its EP roster
onebit_ep_proof a two-node graph (MatMul then Relu) built in memory through the Model Editor API runs with the plugin EP registered first and the CPU EP last, our EP takes the MatMul (the trace has a matmul line, which only Compute can write), and the result matches the CPU EP
onebit_ep_proof_cpu_fallback with ONEBIT_EP_OPS=none the same graph is partitioned to the CPU EP (claimed=0), so the match above cannot come from the CPU running both sessions

onebit_npu_gemm_probe (NPU builds only) is registered as a fourth test and skips when the device is busy rather than failing someone else's run.

Status#

The host path is done: it is what the tests assert, and it needs no hardware. The NPU path is proven on XDNA 2 as well — the ELF loads, ORT hands the EP the MatMul, the kernel runs on the device, and three consecutive runs give the same answer inside the int8 tolerance: max_abs = 9.893e-02 against max|ref| = 20.414 (rel 4.846e-03, gate 2e-2), with the probe's scale fit at 0.9999. What is not done is coverage: an ELF exists per (M, K, N), so on a real model the EP takes the shapes it has a kernel for and the CPU EP takes the rest (for Qwen3-0.6B that is q, k and v). The device backend is still off by default and is not part of any release, because enabling it on a box where another process owns the NPU must stay an explicit decision.

The A8W8 QDQ pattern is claimed and proven (ctest -R onebit_ep_qdq_proof, exact int8 match); the fused form that skips the dequantise/quantise pairs is designed, not built.

The two-engine order is implemented and exercised with a single library; a second EP library was not available to try it against (this ORT build ships no ROCM/HIP EP and there is no gfx1201 HIP EP plugin on the box), so treat a real NPU+GPU session as designed but unmeasured.

The ops list is deliberately one entry long. A plugin EP that claims a node it cannot run makes a graph fail where it used to work, so ops are added only with a passing proof beside them.

Not part of this, and never linked or shipped here: AMD's VitisAI execution provider wheel. This engine talks to the NPU through its own runtime (Releases), and an ORT graph served by 1bit executes our EP's kernels, not VitisAI's.
